provenance.notes: Written for the GM or business development lead at a multi-office restoration company. Leans on adjuster-facing documentation, referral partner portals, large-loss and commercial plans, reconstruction and hiring. No carrier, programme or certification body is named. Carrier portal and consolidator prices are the least certain.

pageStructurePlus.contains: What every restoration file includes (moisture maps, daily drying logs, photo sets by room, itemised estimates), bracketed certifications and insurance details for the office to fill, and a named contact per office
pageStructurePlus.why: Adjusters and agents look up the company before approving a crew. A page written for them answers the questions they would otherwise ask on the phone.

pageStructurePlus.section: Referral partner loss submission and status
pageStructurePlus.contains: A sign-in for agents, plumbers and property managers to submit a water or fire loss, attach the customer's consent, and follow the job from first visit to dry-out and rebuild
pageStructurePlus.why: Most restoration work arrives through referrers. The company that lets them see progress without calling keeps getting the next loss.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Multi-unit and commercial buildings, crew and drying equipment capacity, generators, temporary power and climate control, after-hours contacts, and an emergency response plan sign-up for facility managers
pageStructurePlus.why: Facility managers choose a restoration vendor before the loss, not during it. They want proof of capacity and a plan on file.

pageStructurePlus.section: Office pages with crews and coverage
pageStructurePlus.contains: Each office with the towns its crews cover, the on-call contact, local flood and storm history in brackets for the office to confirm, and recent mitigation jobs nearby
pageStructurePlus.why: Homeowners and adjusters both want the crew closest to the loss. A page per office shows real local presence.

pageStructurePlus.contains: How the same company handles drying, demolition, mold remediation and the rebuild, one project manager from first visit to final walkthrough, typical stages and who signs off each one
pageStructurePlus.why: Families dread juggling a second contractor after the water is gone. Showing one team through the rebuild keeps the larger part of the claim.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Water damage technicians, fire and smoke crews, project managers and estimators by office, the on-call rota explained honestly, training and certification support, and a short phone application
pageStructurePlus.why: Crews are the limit on how many losses a restoration company can take after a storm. Candidates want to know about nights, travel and training.

designDirections.name: Night Shift
designDirections.bestFor: Restoration companies whose first job is answering water and fire losses at night and routing them to the nearest crew
designDirections.headlineSample: Water or fire damage in {City}? A crew is on call tonight
designDirections.whyItFits: A dark, on-call palette with amber accents reads like a monitoring screen. It suits a company selling readiness at the worst hour of someone's year.

designDirections.name: Adjuster Ready
designDirections.bestFor: Multi-office restoration companies that win work through adjusters, agents and property managers as much as homeowners
designDirections.headlineSample: Restoration files adjusters approve, from crews across {City}
designDirections.whyItFits: The family's own combo, used for capability rather than panic: mono labels for documentation, offices and capacity speak to the professionals who send the work.

designDirections.name: Large Loss Partner
designDirections.bestFor: Restoration companies chasing commercial, multi-unit and high-value residential losses with a reconstruction division
designDirections.headlineSample: Large-loss restoration and rebuild for {City} properties
designDirections.whyItFits: A high-trust advisory palette with a serif heading slows the reader down, which suits facility managers and owners choosing a partner for a loss they hope never happens.

openers.line: Adjusters and agents look up a restoration company before they approve the crew, and your site reads like a homeowner brochure. A page on how your water damage files are documented speaks to the people who sign off the claim.
openers.hook: Check whether the site says anything to insurance professionals: documentation, certifications, a named contact. Note what's missing.
openers.linkLine: A restoration page written for adjusters and agents: {demo-link}

openers.line: Plumbers and insurance agents clearly send you water damage jobs, but there's no way for them to submit a loss online and see how it's going. Referrers keep sending work to the restoration company that keeps them informed.
openers.hook: Look for posts thanking a plumber or agent, or reviews mentioning a referral. Then check the site for any partner page.
openers.linkLine: A referral partner portal for restoration losses: {demo-link}

openers.line: You run restoration crews out of more than one office, but the site has a single contact page. A flooded basement in the far town should reach the crew nearest it, not a shared inbox.
openers.hook: Check the listings and site footer for more than one office address. If they share one form, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: Restoration office pages that route each loss to the nearest crew: {demo-link}

openers.line: You've had water damage technician and project manager ads up for a while, and the site has no careers page. Good restoration techs choose the company that explains the on-call rota and training honestly.
openers.hook: Find their job ads and note the roles. Then check the site menu for Careers.
openers.linkLine: A restoration careers page that's straight about nights and travel: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your posts show a flooded office floor and a smoke-damaged warehouse, but the site only talks to homeowners. Facility managers want to see large-loss restoration capacity before they put you in their emergency plan.
openers.hook: Find a commercial or multi-unit job in their posts. Then look for a commercial section on the site.
openers.linkLine: A commercial and large-loss restoration section: {demo-link}

openers.line: The site covers drying out the water and then stops. Homeowners want to know who rebuilds the kitchen after mitigation, and you have a reconstruction crew they can't see.
openers.hook: Look for rebuild or reconstruction work in their posts or the company name. Then check whether the site mentions it.
openers.linkLine: Mitigation through rebuild, one restoration company: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your restoration site is slow on mobile data and the emergency number sits under a large banner. Someone standing in water at midnight is scrolling for that number with wet hands.
openers.hook: Load the site on your phone with wifi off and note where the number appears. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: The restoration site with the emergency line first: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your reviews keep naming project managers who walked families through the insurance side of a water damage claim. That belongs on the restoration site beside the claim steps, not only on the map.
openers.hook: Copy a review that names a project manager. Quote it back when they reply.
openers.linkLine: Restoration reviews placed beside the claim steps: {demo-link}

openers.line: After a big storm, every search for flood cleanup in {City} fills with national ads. A restoration company with a page for that storm and an intake form that works still catches the calls.
openers.hook: Use this the week a major storm or flood is forecast, or the days after one. Name the storm by its date.
openers.linkLine: A storm-response restoration page ready before the rain: {demo-link}

openers.line: Mold remediation gets one short paragraph on your site. People worried about mold read a lot before calling, and the restoration company that explains testing, containment and clearance earns the job.
openers.hook: Find the mold section and note how much it says. Check for testing, containment and clearance wording.
openers.linkLine: A mold remediation page that explains the whole process: {demo-link}

openers.line: Fire and smoke work is folded into the water damage page. After a fire, families need to know about soot, odour, their belongings and where they'll stay, and that deserves its own restoration page.
openers.hook: Check the services menu for a separate fire and smoke page. If it's shared with water, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: A fire and smoke restoration page for families: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your trucks carry industry certification marks, but the site never says what they mean. Adjusters and property managers look for that before they send a restoration job.
openers.hook: Check truck lettering in their posts for certification marks. Note them, but never claim one you didn't see.
openers.linkLine: Restoration certifications and insurance explained plainly: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your posts from the warehouse show a contents pack-out operation, but there's no page explaining pack-out, cleaning and storage. After water or fire damage, families worry about their belongings almost as much as the house.
openers.hook: Look for warehouse, pack-out or contents posts. Then check the site for a contents page.
openers.linkLine: A contents pack-out page for restoration clients: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your contact form promises a reply during business hours, which reads oddly for a restoration company that runs around the clock. The water keeps spreading while the form waits.
openers.hook: Read the wording around their contact form and the thank-you note. Quote it back if they reply.
openers.linkLine: A water damage intake that reaches on-call at any hour: {demo-link}

openers.line: That {specific recent job} you posted shows a well-run restoration job, containment up and drying equipment set out properly. It deserves a case page an adjuster can read, not a post that's gone by next week.
openers.hook: Pick the newest commercial or large residential loss they posted and name it exactly. Skip any job that shows a family or a house number.
openers.linkLine: That restoration job written up as a case page: {demo-link}

sequence.dm1:
Hi {Owner}, I was looking at restoration companies around {City} and {Business Name} stood out: several offices, a lot of water and fire work, and clearly plenty of referrals from agents and plumbers. The site, though, talks only to homeowners and gives referrers no way to send a loss or follow it.

I put together a sample built for a company your size: an adjuster page, a referral partner portal and office pages routed to the nearest crew, with marked placeholders where your photos would go.

Who looks after the website on your side?
sequence.dm2:
{Owner}, following up in case my note got buried under losses. Here's the sample restoration site for {Business Name}: {demo-link}

Worth a look: a page for adjusters on how your files are documented, a portal where agents and plumbers submit a loss and see its status, office pages, a large-loss section and a careers page for techs. Happy to send it to your business development lead instead.
sequence.call:
"Hi, is this {Owner}? I'm {Your Name}, I build websites and partner portals for restoration companies around {City}. I sent you a sample site this week, did it reach you?"

IF NO:
"No problem, your phones are busier than most. Short version: I rebuilt the {Business Name} site as a sample with a page for adjusters, a referral portal for agents and plumbers, office pages and a large-loss section, with marked placeholders where your photos would go. Who should I email it to?"

IF YES:
"What stood out to you?"
 → let them talk, don't fill the silence
"This doesn't replace your job management system or any carrier programme. It's the public site and the partner portal on top of them, and you own it. The build runs {Build Range} depending on offices, divisions and how far the portal connects to your job files, then {Care Range} a month for hosting, changes and keeping it connected. For a company your size I'd quote about {Build Price}."
"Could we do twenty minutes with you and whoever manages your referral partners?"

CLOSE:
"I'll send a one-page scope for the owners. We launch the adjuster page and office pages first, then the portal."

objections.objection: Most of our work comes through carrier programmes.
objections.handler: "Programme work still gets checked; adjusters and desk reviewers look you up. And the direct and referral work is the part you control. The adjuster page serves the first, the partner portal grows the second."

objections.objection: Our job management software already has a portal.
objections.handler: "Then I connect to it rather than duplicate it. Most of those portals are built for adjusters already on the file. Mine is the front door for agents, plumbers and managers sending you their next restoration job."

objections.objection: We can't promise response times on a website.
objections.handler: "Agreed, and nothing on the site will. It explains the process and who to call, and you approve every line. Any timing wording is yours, in brackets until you confirm it."

objections.objection: The owners and the ops director make this call.
objections.handler: "Of course. I'll send a one-page scope they can read quickly, and I'm glad to walk all of you through it together in twenty minutes."

objections.objection: After a storm we can't take on anything else.
objections.handler: "Then we build in a quiet stretch so it's ready before the next one. I need about two hours of your team's time across the project, mostly approving pages."
"{Build Range}, depending on offices, divisions and how deep the portal goes. For your company I'd quote about {Build Price}, which is in the range of one mid-size water damage claim."

email.subject: Adjuster page and partner portal for {Business Name}

sequence.voicemail: "Hi {Owner}, it's {Your Name}. I build websites and partner portals for restoration companies around {City}, and I've put together a sample for {Business Name}, with an adjuster page and a referral portal. I'll email the link. {Your Phone}. Thanks."
sequence.takedown:
{Owner}, I'm clearing sample sites on Friday, the {Business Name} restoration one included.

Should I keep it up for your team to review, or let it go? One word back is fine.
sequence.nurture:
Hi {Owner}, storm season is close, which is when restoration companies find out whether their intake and referral paths hold up.

The adjuster page and partner portal sample is still here: {demo-link}. I can add any offices you've opened since we spoke.

bullets: Peg the build to one mid-size water damage claim, not to page count. Restoration leaders think in claims and referral partners.
Price the referral partner portal as its own line; how much it reads from their job system sets the price.
Office pages are priced per office, and only for offices with their own crews and on-call contact.
Keep anything an adjuster might read factual and approved by the owner; allow review time for it in the scope.
Large-loss and commercial pages are a separate line, because they need capacity details and an emergency plan sign-up.
Never write response-time promises or name carriers; that is the client's wording to supply.

lineItems.description: Max with sample documentation sets, bracketed certifications per office and a named contact for each office.

lineItems.item: Referral partner loss submission and status portal
lineItems.description: Max when partners see live job stages pulled from the job management system and get updates without calling.

lineItems.item: Office page with crews and coverage (each)
lineItems.description: Max with the office's towns, on-call contact, local jobs and loss intake routed to that office.

lineItems.item: Commercial large-loss and emergency plan section
lineItems.description: Max with capacity details, a plan sign-up form that collects building contacts and shut-off locations, and a facility manager contact path.
Max when it launches within a day of the storm with its own intake form and office routing.

lineItems.item: Careers section for techs, PMs and estimators
lineItems.description: Max with roles per office, an honest on-call page, crew video placeholders and applications routed by role.
Max with stage-by-stage write-ups from mitigation to final walkthrough, with written owner consent for any photos.

lineItems.item: Loss intake form routed to on-call
lineItems.description: Max when it asks the loss type, source and affected rooms, then pages the on-call person for that office.

whatElseYouSell.name: Partner newsletter for agents and plumbers
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Each month your referral partners get a short note: a case from their area, a water damage tip they can pass on and a reminder of how to send a loss."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 2, once the partner portal is live.

whatElseYouSell.name: Review requests after each closed claim
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "When a restoration job closes, the family gets a review request naming the project manager, and the good ones land on the office page that served them."
whatElseYouSell.when: Day 30, once office pages are live.

whatElseYouSell.name: Office listings management
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Each restoration office keeps its own listing current: towns covered, on-call number, storm notices and new case posts, so the map sends a loss to the nearest crew."

whatElseYouSell.name: Storm response ad and page kit
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A storm page, ad copy and listing posts prepared in advance, so when flooding hits the region your restoration intake is live the same day."
whatElseYouSell.when: Before storm season, refreshed each year.

whatElseYouSell.name: Lunch-and-learn deck for insurance agents
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A short deck and handout your business development team presents at agency offices: what happens after a water loss, what to tell the policyholder and how to send it to you."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 2, once the adjuster page and portal are live.

whatElseYouSell.name: Large-loss capability brochure and video
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A capability brochure and short video showing crews, drying equipment and generators on a commercial loss, for the business development team to leave with facility managers."
whatElseYouSell.when: Once they want more commercial restoration accounts.

whatElseYouSell.name: Technician recruiting campaign
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A recruiting push aimed at people who'd make good water damage technicians, landing on a careers page that's honest about nights, travel and training."
whatElseYouSell.when: When they post several tech openings, or before storm season.

whatElseYouSell.name: Facility manager emergency-plan campaign
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "An email sequence and meeting invite inviting facility managers to put a restoration emergency plan on file before the next flood or fire."
whatElseYouSell.when: Once the large-loss section and plan sign-up are live.

withoutAI.route: Flooring and cabinet supplier for the rebuild
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The supplier your reconstruction crew buys flooring and cabinets from needs a catalogue site with trade accounts. Your introduction after a big order opens the door."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Suppliers sell to every restoration rebuild and remodel crew in town and rarely have a usable trade site.

withoutAI.route: Environmental testing lab for mold and asbestos
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The lab that tests for mold and asbestos before your crews open walls needs a site where homeowners and contractors book sampling. Your mold page links to them."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Independent testing keeps the remediation honest, so testers and restoration companies refer to each other constantly.

withoutAI.route: Moving and storage firm for long pack-outs
withoutAI.whoPays: The moving and storage company, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "When a fire job needs contents stored for months, the storage company you use needs a site that explains insurance-paid storage. I'll build it at my normal rate."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Movers who handle restoration contents rarely explain that work online, and your referral is a warm introduction.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The condo managers you dry out buildings for need a resident portal for notices and requests. I build it, and water damage reports route to your restoration team."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Multi-unit water losses spread between units, and managers already rely on the restoration company that handled the last one.

withoutAI.whoPays: The roofing contractor, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "After a storm, the roofer tarps it and your crew dries the inside. That roofer needs a storm page as much as you do, and both sites can point to each other."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Roof leaks and interior water damage arrive together, so the two companies already pass jobs back and forth.

withoutAI.route: Temporary housing provider for displaced families
withoutAI.pitchLine: "Families whose homes you're restoring after a fire need somewhere to stay. The housing provider you work with needs a site and request form adjusters can use."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Housing providers live on restoration and adjuster referrals and are a short introduction away.

withAI.route: Loss notice drafter for condo managers
withAI.pitchLine: "When a pipe bursts on an upper floor, the manager gets draft notices for affected residents and the board, with the restoration contact and next steps filled in."
withAI.whyItWorks: Managers write the same urgent notices after every water loss and want them right the first time.

withAI.route: Lab result explainer for the testing company
withAI.pitchLine: "Mold and air sample results become a plain summary for the homeowner, drafted from the lab's own notes and signed off by their assessor, with no health claims."
withAI.whyItWorks: Testers spend hours explaining results by phone, and clearer reports bring more remediation referrals.

withAI.route: Rebuild finish matcher for the supplier
withAI.whoPays: The flooring and cabinet supplier, monthly
withAI.pitchLine: "Rebuild crews upload a sample of the damaged floor or cabinet door and the supplier's assistant suggests close matches in stock for the restoration estimate."
withAI.whyItWorks: Matching finishes slows every rebuild. Suppliers that solve it win the order from every restoration company.

withAI.route: Placement request sorter for the housing provider
withAI.pitchLine: "Requests from adjusters and restoration project managers are sorted by family size, pets, school area and dates, so the housing team matches homes faster."
withAI.whyItWorks: Housing providers juggle many urgent requests after a big fire or flood; faster matching keeps adjusters loyal.

withAI.route: Storm damage intake for the roofing partner
withAI.pitchLine: "The roofer gets the same storm intake your restoration team uses, sorting roof leaks from interior water damage so each job goes to the right crew."
withAI.whyItWorks: You've built it once for restoration, so the second build is configuration, and both companies share the storm calls.

withAI.route: Field report drafts for independent adjusting firms
withAI.pitchLine: "Independent adjusters dictate notes on site and get a draft field report on their template, with water damage and fire findings ordered the way the carrier wants."
withAI.whyItWorks: Adjusting firms are buried in reports after a storm, and they already know which restoration companies run tidy files.

softwareAI.name: Loss intake text-back and on-call paging
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Any missed call or half-finished intake gets a text asking the loss type and address, and water or fire losses page the on-call restoration lead straight away."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Day 30. Needs their numbers, the on-call rota per office and approved wording.

softwareAI.name: Review replies for each office
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every review gets a reply drafted in the company voice, careful about claim details, naming the project manager and the restoration work, for the office manager to approve."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs a set of past replies and an approver per office. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Referral source report by agent and plumber
softwareAI.pitchLine: "See which agents, plumbers and managers send restoration losses, what each loss was worth and who's gone quiet, so business development visits the right people."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs job records with referral source and invoice totals.

softwareAI.name: Claim milestone portal for homeowners and adjusters
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Homeowners and adjusters log in to see where the restoration job stands: drying, demolition, estimate approved, rebuild scheduled, with documents attached to each stage."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs read access to the job management system and their list of job stages.

softwareAI.name: Around-the-clock loss intake agent
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It answers every call the office can't, asks the source of the water or fire, the rooms affected and the insurance details, and pages the nearest restoration crew."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs on-call rotas per office, intake questions and safety wording they approve. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Drying equipment pool across offices
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every dehumidifier, air mover and generator across the offices on one list, with which job it's on and when it's due back, so a big loss can borrow from another office."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs their equipment list with tags and how jobs are logged.

softwareAI.name: Daily job updates to homeowner and adjuster
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Each evening the homeowner and adjuster get a short update on the restoration job: readings taken, equipment on site, what happens tomorrow."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs job stage data and approved message templates.

softwareAI.name: File completeness checker before submission
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Before a water damage file goes to the adjuster, it checks for missing moisture readings, room photos, signatures and daily logs, and lists what to fix."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs a sample of approved and rejected files and the checklist they use. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Commercial emergency response plan builder
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Facility managers fill in contacts, shut-off locations and priorities for each building, and the restoration team gets a plan it can act on the night of a loss."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs their current plan template and a pilot commercial client.

softwareAI.name: Supplement request drafts for estimators
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When hidden water damage turns up behind a wall, the estimator gets a supplement request drafted with the photos, readings and reasons in the order adjusters expect."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs past supplements that were approved and their estimate format. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Receivables board by carrier and adjuster
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every unpaid restoration invoice grouped by carrier, adjuster and age, with the last contact and next step, so the office chases the right files first."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs an export of open invoices and payer details.

softwareAI.name: Mold and fire questions assistant on the site
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It answers questions about mold remediation, smoke odour and the claim process from your own pages, gives no health advice, and hands urgent losses to on-call."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs their process pages and approved answers. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Reconstruction schedule and trade board
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every rebuild after mitigation on one board: drywall, flooring, cabinets and paint by trade and date, so project managers stop rebuilding the schedule by phone."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs their rebuild stages, trade partners and how they schedule today.

softwareAI.name: Job photo tagging by room and drying stage
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Crews upload hundreds of photos per water damage job; it tags each by room and stage, so the file reads in order and nothing is missing at review."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs a sample of past job photo sets. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer; staff confirm the tags.

softwareAI.name: Referral thank-you and status updates
softwareAI.pitchLine: "The agent or plumber who sent the loss gets a thank-you and short updates as the restoration job moves, without anyone in the office remembering to call."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, with the partner portal. Needs referral sources on job records.

softwareAI.name: Office scorecard on cycle time, margin and reviews
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Each restoration office on one page: losses taken, days to dry-out, file approval rate, margin by loss type and reviews, refreshed weekly."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 8. Needs read access to the job system and billing, and the measures leadership already tracks.

softwareAI.name: Applicant screen for techs and project managers
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Applicants answer questions on night calls, travel for storms, driving record and restoration experience, and each office manager sees a short ranked list."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: With the careers section. Needs must-haves by role and pay bands. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Storm surge intake triage
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When a storm floods hundreds of homes at once, it sorts every intake by water source, depth and vulnerable occupants, so crews reach the worst losses first."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Before storm season. Needs intake data from past storms and their priority rules. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Crew training and certification tracker
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every technician's restoration certifications, renewal dates and completed training in one place, so offices know who can lead a mold or fire job."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 7. Needs their training records and the certifications they track.

softwareAI.name: Weather alerts to emergency plan holders
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When heavy rain or flooding is forecast near {City}, every commercial client with a restoration plan on file gets a checklist and a direct line to their office."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6, once plans are on file. Needs a weather feed and approved checklist wording.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "I built a file checker for one multi-office restoration company. Every restorer loses money on water damage files that come back for missing readings."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Rejected files are a shared pain, and the first client paid to learn what adjusters reject.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The holding group buying restoration companies
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Every restoration company you acquire brings its own site, intake and referral habits. One platform with a page set per brand and shared intake folds them in."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Consolidators repeat the same integration after every deal and pay for one that already works.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Each franchise office needs local pages, an adjuster page and intake routed to its own on-call crew. I've built that for a multi-office restorer already."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Franchise systems buy per office, turning one template into many builds.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The insurance carrier's claims operations team
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your preferred restoration vendors submit files in different ways. A shared portal with consistent milestones and documentation saves your desk adjusters hours."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Carriers spend heavily on claim handling time, and a working vendor portal from a real restorer is credible proof.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your network restorers need one intake, one milestone format and one place to upload water damage files. I've built that layer for one of them."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Administrators sell speed and consistency to carriers, and vendor tooling is how they prove it.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Drying equipment maker's contractor training portal
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your restoration contractors need training videos, equipment registration and support requests in one portal. Your best customers are the ones who'd use it."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Equipment makers fund contractor education to sell more units, and a restorer client opens the door.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The regional or national restoration association
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Offer members an adjuster page template and a careers kit built for restoration companies. Documentation and hiring are what every member struggles with."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Associations need benefits members use, and these two topics fill every conference agenda.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The marketing agency, per restoration client
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your agency runs ads for restoration companies but builds pages only for homeowners. License my adjuster page, office pages and partner portal per client."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Agencies hold many restoration accounts and lack the industry knowledge to build the professional side.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Property management group's multi-site emergency plans
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Across your buildings, flood and fire plans live in binders. One portal holds every site's plan, contacts and restoration vendor, and alerts the right people."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Large portfolios carry real risk and pay for preparedness; the restoration client is the introduction.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Campus or hospital facilities vendor portal
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The university or hospital facilities department
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your facilities team needs one place to log water leaks, call the restoration vendor and keep the documentation for each building. I've built the vendor side already."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Large campuses have frequent leaks, strict documentation and budgets for tools that save staff time.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: A restoration company in another region, at your normal rate
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "I work with one multi-crew restoration company per region. {City} is taken; the next region's leading restorer is open."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Restoration owners meet at training events and storm deployments, and exclusivity helps them decide.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The storm response network or coalition
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "When restoration crews travel to a disaster, they need shared intake, crew rosters and job maps. I've built storm intake for one company and can extend it to the network."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Catastrophe deployments are chaotic and short of tools, and member companies share the cost.

upsellLadder.offer: Restoration site, adjuster page and portal plus care
upsellLadder.trigger: The owners approve the one-page scope.
upsellLadder.line: "The restoration site, adjuster page, partner portal and care go on one contract, so a new office or on-call change is an email to me."

upsellLadder.offer: Review requests after each closed claim
upsellLadder.trigger: The first restoration jobs close since launch and families thank a project manager by name.
upsellLadder.line: "Families are thanking your project managers. Let's turn each closed water damage job into a review on that office's page."

upsellLadder.offer: Loss intake text-back and on-call paging
upsellLadder.trigger: Call logs show missed calls or abandoned intake forms at night.
upsellLadder.line: "Some losses called and didn't get through. A text back and a page to on-call keeps those restoration jobs from going elsewhere."

upsellLadder.offer: Referral source report by agent and plumber
upsellLadder.trigger: Partners start submitting losses through the portal.
upsellLadder.line: "Agents and plumbers are using the portal. Now let's see which referrers send the best restoration losses and who's gone quiet."

upsellLadder.trigger: They mention files coming back from adjusters for missing items.
upsellLadder.line: "Files keep coming back for missing readings. A check before each water damage file goes out stops that."

upsellLadder.offer: Claim milestone portal for homeowners and adjusters
upsellLadder.trigger: Project managers say they spend hours a day on status calls.
upsellLadder.line: "Your project managers are answering status calls all day. A portal that shows every restoration milestone gives them that time back."

upsellLadder.trigger: Several facility managers have asked for a plan through the large-loss section.
upsellLadder.line: "Facility managers are asking for plans. Let's give them a builder that puts every building's restoration plan on file."

upsellLadder.offer: Office scorecard on cycle time, margin and reviews
upsellLadder.trigger: They open or acquire another office.
upsellLadder.line: "With another restoration office coming on, leadership needs every office on one page: losses, dry-out time, file approvals and margin."
